title: Endpoint Routing Internals
description: Deep dive into endpoint routing, route matching algorithms, endpoint metadata, and how to extend the routing system with custom conventions and filters.

data.text: Endpoint routing is the system that matches an incoming URL to an endpoint and then executes the associated handler. Introduced in ASP.NET Core 3.0, it replaced the older IRouter-based system and unified routing for both MVC and minimal APIs. Understanding its internals helps you diagnose 404s, optimize route tables, and build advanced routing behaviors.

An **endpoint** in ASP.NET Core is more than a URL pattern. It is an object that contains a route pattern, a request delegate, metadata (such as authorization or CORS policies), and display information. When a request arrives, the routing middleware compares it against the endpoint table and selects the best match.

The route matcher uses a sophisticated algorithm that considers the HTTP method, path, and any route constraints. It processes endpoints in the order they were added, picking the first one that matches. Once a match is found, the endpoint is stored in `HttpContext.GetEndpoint()` so downstream middleware can inspect it.

data.title: Route matching inputs
items: HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.)
Request path and query string (query parameters do not affect matching unless used in constraints)
Route values extracted from the path pattern
Metadata attached to the endpoint, such as authorization policies or output formatters

data.title: Minimal API endpoint with route constraints
data.content: Endpoints support inline constraints such as int, bool, and datetime.

data.text: Endpoints carry metadata that influences how they are processed. For example, `[Authorize]` adds an authorization policy to the endpoint metadata. `RequireCors` adds CORS policy names. You can read this metadata in middleware or apply it dynamically using endpoint filters.

data.title: Reading endpoint metadata in middleware
data.content: Inspect endpoint metadata before the endpoint executes.

data.title: Endpoint Metadata is Powerful
data.text: Endpoint metadata decouples routing from behavior. Instead of hardcoding checks in every controller or minimal API handler, you can write a single middleware or filter that inspects metadata and enforces policies, rate limits, or feature flags.

cards.title: Endpoint Routing
cards.description: The modern system introduced in ASP.NET Core 3.0.
pros: Unified routing for MVC and minimal APIs
Better performance with compiled route matchers
cons: Steeper learning curve for advanced scenarios
Requires explicit UseRouting and UseEndpoints calls in some hosting models

cards.title: Legacy IRouter
cards.description: The older routing system used before ASP.NET Core 3.0.
cons: Separate systems for MVC and Web API
No built-in metadata or endpoint filters
Slower route matching for large route tables

data.title: Endpoint Routing Summary
points: Endpoint routing matches requests to endpoint objects that carry route patterns, handlers, and metadata.
The matcher considers HTTP method, path, and constraints in registration order.
Endpoint metadata enables cross-cutting behavior like authorization, CORS, and rate limiting.
Endpoint filters provide a way to run code before or after an endpoint handler.
Modern ASP.NET Core uses endpoint routing; legacy IRouter is obsolete.
data.takeaway: Endpoint routing is the central nervous system of request dispatch in ASP.NET Core. By understanding how routes are matched and how metadata flows through the system, you can build more maintainable and performant applications.
